title: What Are Perpetual Futures In Crypto?
summary: A crypto perpetual is a derivative that tracks the price of an underlying asset like bitcoin, letting traders take a position on where the price is headed without ever holding the asset itself.
body_markdown:
Most futures contracts come with an expiration date. Perpetual futures, as the name suggests, don't. That single design choice turned them into one of the most heavily traded instruments in crypto.


A crypto perpetual is a derivative that tracks the price of an underlying asset like bitcoin, letting traders take a position on where the price is headed without ever holding the asset itself. What keeps a contract that never settles from drifting away from the real market is a mechanism called funding: at regular intervals, traders on the more crowded side of the trade pay those on the other. When the perpetual trades above spot, longs pay shorts; when it trades below, shorts pay longs. The result is a contract that hugs the spot price indefinitely, with no expiry, no rollover, and no settlement date to manage.


For institutions, that structure does real work. Positions can be opened and adjusted around the clock, hedges can be held for as long as the risk lasts rather than reset every quarter, and deep perpetual order books often carry the tightest liquidity in the crypto market.


This article breaks down how crypto perpetual futures actually work, how they stack up against traditional futures and options, why they came to dominate crypto derivatives, and the structural risks institutions should weigh before using them. For a wider view of the landscape, see BitGo's[Crypto Derivatives 101](https://www.bitgo.com/resources/blog/crypto-derivatives-101/) which covers futures, options, and perpetuals together.


## Key Takeaways


-


Perpetual futures track an asset like bitcoin and, unlike every other futures contract, never expire, which is exactly why they dominate crypto trading volume.


-


A funding mechanism keeps the contract tethered to spot: whichever side of the trade is more crowded pays the other, at regular intervals, indefinitely.


-


Against traditional futures, perpetuals drop the quarterly rollover entirely, so a position can stay open as long as the thesis holds.


-


Against options, perpetuals give direct, linear price exposure, with none of the volatility-and-time pricing math that governs an option's value.


-


For institutions, the real diligence is in the mechanics: funding rates, margin and liquidation rules, liquidity depth, counterparty exposure, and custody.


## Crypto Perpetuals: The Basics


A crypto perpetual is a derivative whose value shadows the price of a digital asset, letting a trader go long or short without ever touching the underlying token in the spot market.


You'll see them called perpetual swaps, perpetual futures, crypto perpetuals, or just perps. Venues don't use the terms identically, but the defining trait never changes: a perpetual is built to stay open with no scheduled expiration date.


That's the clean break from a traditional futures contract, which has a fixed maturity and a settlement process waiting at the end of it. A perpetual has neither. It can stay open as long as the holder meets margin requirements and the venue keeps the market running.


In principle, the instrument is a hedging tool, a way to offset the risk in an existing position without unwinding it. In practice, crypto traders have spent years using perps as something blunter: a high-leverage directional bet on where the market is going next. Both uses run on the same contract, which is part of what makes it so versatile. For an institution, that versatility shows up as several distinct jobs the same product can do: take a directional view, hedge a spot holding, provide liquidity, or run funding-rate arbitrage and delta-neutral strategies. What it really changes is the full lifecycle of crypto exposure, how it's created, margined, financed, and monitored.


Which leads to the question that actually matters: does the contract's funding, margin, liquidity, and custody model fit the institution's risk framework?


## How Crypto Perpetual Futures Work


By now the what is clear, so this is the how. Two mechanisms do the real work: funding keeps the price honest, and margin keeps the position alive.


Start with funding, the cleverer of the two. A perpetual has no expiry to force its price back in line with spot, so the market manufactures the pressure itself. When the contract trades above spot, longs pay shorts a periodic fee; when it trades below, shorts pay longs. Either way, the crowded side is taxed and the empty side is paid, which nudges traders to lean against the imbalance until the gap closes. The rate floats with how wide that gap is, so a perpetual running hot above spot carries a steeper funding cost than one trading a hair off. Exact formulas, intervals, and calculation methods differ by venue, but the logic is identical everywhere: pay traders to push the price back toward the reference market.


Margin is the less glamorous half, and the one that ends positions. To open and hold a perpetual, a trader posts collateral. If the price moves against the position hard enough to drag that collateral below the maintenance threshold, the venue can liquidate, closing the position to cover the shortfall whether or not the trader wants out. For an institution, that turns margin from a setup step into a live monitoring problem, because the funding clock and the liquidation threshold are both ticking the entire time a position is open.


So while a perpetual can in theory stay open forever, in practice it lasts exactly as long as the holder keeps funding, margin, liquidity, and operations under control. Lose the thread on any one of them and the position closes itself.


Crypto Perpetuals vs Futures vs Options


All three are derivatives, but they hand the trader very different shapes of risk.


Perpetuals and traditional futures are close cousins. Both are linear: the position gains or loses roughly dollar-for-dollar with the underlying, up when you're long and the asset rises, down when it falls. The one thing separating them is the calendar. A traditional future matures, so the position has to be settled, closed, or rolled into the next contract, and that roll is operational work that lands at the worst possible time, when markets are moving fast. A perpetual never matures, so there's no roll to manage. The catch is that you trade the expiry problem for the funding problem: a position that looks great on direction can quietly incur heavy funding costs over time.


Options break the pattern entirely. An option is the right, not the obligation, to buy or sell at a set strike, and that optionality bends the payoff into a curve instead of a straight line. Because the holder can walk away, the price of an option reflects far more than which way spot is pointing. It prices in implied volatility, time to expiration, and how far the strike sits from the current market price. Buy an option and the most you can lose is the premium, but you're now betting on volatility and racing the clock of time decay.


So the choice comes down to the shape of the trade. Want clean, leveraged exposure to direction with no expiry to babysit? That's perpetual. Need a hard-capped downside or a payoff that only pays past a certain level? That's an option, with the volatility and decay math that comes attached. The instrument follows the objective, not the other way around.


## Why Crypto Perpetuals Became Dominant In Derivatives Markets


Crypto perpetuals became prominent because their structure fits the operating rhythm of digital asset markets. Crypto spot markets trade continuously. Price moves can occur overnight, on weekends, and across global trading sessions. A derivative with no fixed expiration is naturally aligned with this market structure.


The absence of contract expiration also reduces roll friction. In dated futures markets, participants must manage exposure across maturities. That can introduce basis risk, liquidity differences, and operational complexity. Perpetuals concentrate all this activity into a single continuously traded instrument instead of spreading it across several expiration dates.


Liquidity concentration reinforced adoption. When more traders and market makers use the same contract, spreads become tighter and execution becomes more predictable. This does not make the product low-risk per se, but it does make the product operationally useful for institutions that need fast and capital efficient access to long or short exposure.


Perpetuals also make funding visible. The funding rate provides a market signal about demand for long or short exposure. Institutions can use that information as part of a broader market structure review, usually combining it with other data points to create a coherent market view.


The result is a derivatives market where perpetual futures often function as the primary instrument for continuous directional exposure.


## The Risks Institutions Need to Weigh


The unique dangers in perpetual futures, outside of traditional market risks, typically come from five places: leverage, funding, liquidation, liquidity, and counterparty structure. What makes them genuinely hazardous is that they're wired together. The same violent move that drives up funding costs also drains the collateral on one side of the trade, and the moment you most need to adjust is the moment the liquidity to do it cheaply has evaporated. Risks that look manageable one by one tend to arrive all at once.


Funding is the slow leak. The mechanism itself is covered above; the risk is that it runs against you and keeps running. A trader can be dead right on direction over weeks while the funding cost quietly compounds the entire time they wait to be proven correct. Being early and being wrong can cost about the same.


Liquidation is the sudden one, and it hasn't gone away just because the market has matured. Bitcoin's volatility has trended down from the wild swings of the early years, but perpetuals run on margin, and it doesn't take a 2017-style move to trigger a cascade. When collateral slips under the maintenance threshold, the venue can cut or close the position automatically, with no regard for the trader's longer view, and that still happens regularly, usually in exactly the conditions that caused it: a fast move, a spike in volatility, and an order book that thins out right when the forced exit needs depth.


Spot volatility feeds both. Crypto prices still move fast enough that a perpetual translates every one of those moves straight into marked exposure on the position. Without firm rules for sizing, monitoring, and collateral, a manageable position can turn into an unmanageable one between one check and the next.


Then there's the question of where the money actually sits. Counterparty and custody design sit underneath all of it: where collateral is held, how it's segregated, who has the authority to move it, and what controls govern every transfer. This is why institutions lean on[qualified custody solutions](https://www.bitgo.com/products/qualified-custody/) for regulated, insured, and secure custody of the digital assets backing their positions, so that the collateral layer isn't itself a source of great risk.


## Crypto Perpetuals And The Evolution Of Digital Asset Markets


Perpetuals became a fixture of crypto derivatives on exchanges, where continuous trading and deep liquidity made them a natural fit for a market that never closes. For institutions, though, exchange-traded perps are only one way to manage derivatives exposure. OTC derivatives offer another execution model, allowing trades to be structured around specific risk and return objectives.


BitGo supports institutional derivatives trading through its OTC desk, with custody and collateral management supporting the assets behind those positions. Institutions can also access financing and settlement services through BitGo, connecting derivatives execution with other parts of their digital asset operations.


That connection reflects where the derivatives market is headed. Perpetuals have given institutions another tool for managing continuous exposure, while the growth of OTC markets and the infrastructure around them creates more ways to structure, execute, and manage that exposure. Together, these markets are bringing digital assets closer to the range of tools institutions already use to manage risk across traditional markets.


## FAQs


### What is a perpetual contract in crypto?


It's a derivative that tracks a digital asset's price with no expiration date. Regular funding payments between longs and shorts keep the contract tethered to the spot market in place of a settlement date.


### Are crypto perpetuals the same as futures?


Not quite. They behave like futures and give the same linear, dollar-for-dollar exposure to the underlying, but a traditional future expires on a set date while a perpetual doesn't. Perpetuals use ongoing funding payments to stay aligned with spot instead of settling at maturity.


### What makes perpetuals so popular in crypto?


They fit the way crypto trades. Spot markets run around the clock, and a contract that never expires matches that better than one tied to a calendar. Liquidity also pools into a single contract rather than splitting across expiry dates, and traders can hold a long or short position for as long as they like without rolling into the next contract.


Perpetual futures involve leverage, funding costs, and liquidation risk, and outcomes can vary significantly based on market conditions and how a position is margined and managed.
